title: Decision complexity of weak Presburger arithmetic
formal: Historical question, resolved: does removing order from Presburger arithmetic over the integers lower its decision complexity? The input is a closed first-order formula built from integer linear equalities, Boolean connectives and integer quantifiers. The task is to decide its truth in Z. There is no bound on the number of variables or quantifier alternations. Coefficients and constants are binary encoded. The 2022 result gives weak Presburger arithmetic the same STA(*, 2^{2^{n^{O(1)}}}, O(n)) completeness classification as full Presburger arithmetic, where n is input length.
context:
The 2020 paper primarily asks which sets described using order can also be described without it. Its concluding motivation is a separate question about deciding the truth of arbitrary order-free sentences. A loss of expressive power alone does not imply an easier decision problem.

The source uses all of Z. Restricting to nonnegative integers changes the definability of order, so that alteration would obscure the comparison the authors intended. Binary coefficients are also part of the source model.

Chistikov, Haase, Hadizadeh and Mansutti explicitly settle the longstanding comparison in 2022. Even the positive fragment, using ∧, ∨, ∃ and ∀ without negation, has the required hardness. Weak arithmetic therefore retains the ordered theory’s worst-case classification.

The March 2026 LMCS article cites the 2022 classification for unrestricted weak arithmetic while proving tractability for particular bounded-negation syntaxes. Restrictions on the available connective basis and quantifiers matter when comparing such fragments.
why: Separates expressive weakness from algorithmic simplicity in a basic decidable arithmetic theory used to describe integer constraints.
status_note: Matched the integer domain, binary encoding and unrestricted quantified decision task to the MFCS 2022 result, whose abstract explicitly identifies and answers this question. definitions: An atomic formula has the form a₁x₁+⋯+aₖxₖ=b, with aᵢ,b∈Z. Formulas are finite syntax trees formed using negation, conjunction, disjunction, and quantifiers ∃x and ∀x; a closed formula has no free variables. Quantifiers range over all positive, zero and negative integers. Coefficients multiply variables only by constants: products of two variables are unavailable. The comparison theory, full Presburger arithmetic, additionally permits linear inequalities. The input length counts the syntax and binary representations of all integers. STA(*,t(n),a(n)) denotes languages decided by an alternating Turing machine whose every computation path has at most t(n) steps and a(n) changes between existential and universal states; * imposes no separate space restriction. An existential configuration accepts if some successor accepts and a universal configuration accepts if every successor accepts. Here the time bound is doubly exponential in a polynomial of n and the alternation bound is linear in n; the notation allows fixed constants and a fixed polynomial depending on the deciding machine. The stated classification is an alternating complexity classification, not a claimed matching deterministic running-time formula.
answer_criterion: Determine whether the order-free theory has the same decision-complexity classification as the ordered theory. The published lower bound already holds for positive weak arithmetic and its Horn fragment; containment in full Presburger arithmetic supplies the matching upper classification. This resolves the source question without asserting that arbitrary ordered formulas have equivalent order-free definitions.
